independentDerivations.argument: Choose a positive orientation for the cross-section. Let q be the net signed charge transported across it during a positive finite interval Delta t, so q = integral I(t) dt. Dividing by the interval gives the time average q/Delta t. For constant I the integral is I Delta t, and that average equals the same constant current for every interval. A finite interval does not in general define an instantaneous current. The added average-current explanation is therefore correct without changing equation (9-1).

For one carrier species of charge q0, uniform number density n and mean normal drift velocity v across area S, the net carrier transport in time Delta t is n S v Delta t, with its sign determined by the chosen normal. Hence net transported charge is q0 n S v Delta t and I = q0 n v S. In the source's right-moving example v > 0 and Delta l > 0: N = n S Delta l, q = q0 N and Delta t = Delta l/v give q/Delta t = q0 n S Delta l/(Delta l/v) = q0 n v S. The middle cancellation in (9-2) is correct. Dimensions are C times m^-3 times m/s times m^2 = C/s.

With left-to-right positive, positive carriers drifting right give positive current and positive carriers drifting left give negative current. For electrons q0 = -e with e > 0: rightward electron drift gives I < 0, whereas leftward drift gives I > 0. Conventional current is opposite electron drift. Reversing the selected axis reverses v and I, not q0, e, S, n or the positive elapsed time. Delta t = Delta l/v is used only in the source's v > 0 traversal example, not with a negative v and positive Delta l; the general signed-current relation follows directly from oriented flux.

An ensemble mean does not determine every particle's displacement. As an explicit counterexample, take equal-density subpopulations with normal velocities 0 and 2v, for v > 0. Their mean normal velocity is v and their total net flux is n S v. During Delta l/v, however, the stationary subpopulation originally between the two sections does not reach section 2 at all. The current formula remains correct but the claim that all initially present particles pass section 2 does not follow. Uniform bulk drift is a valid continuum picture, not an assertion about each microscopic trajectory.

findings.whyItFails: The explicit two-subpopulation counterexample above preserves both the mean drift and I = q0 n v S but falsifies the all-particles assertion. The source carries the same simplified wording; its preservation and native errors[] do not make this literal microscopic inference scientifically true.
